display_title: Official Review of Submission12191 by Reviewer sS44

summary.value: This paper proposes FLowDUP to train personalized models for clients participating in federated learning with and for even clients that have unlabeled data using only a forward pass. FLowDUP trains a hypernetwork that takes the unlabeled dataset and outputs parameters of a personalized predictive model that allows them to train in a subspace that is much smaller than the actual underlying personalzied model. They provide intuition behind their method by giving a generalization bound with multi-task PAC-Bayesian. The paper includes experimental evaluation of FLowDUP

strengths.value:
- The paper investigates an important problem in FL where clients without labels can often exist and not be able to gain anything out of federated learning. 
- The paper provides theoretical insights into their proposed algorithm's loss function regarding using labeled clients to benefit the unlabeled client's personalized models. 
- The paper is clearly written.

weaknesses.value:
- FLowDUP relies largely on the labeled clients' data, and due to this I have a couple of concerns. First, if the labeled clients data does not match well of the unlabeled clients' data, which is often the case in federated learning due to data heterogeneity and cannot really be controlled since they are clients' private data, the performance I believe will largely suffer. Moreover, it is rather unfair for the labeled clients to provide their training resource/data for the benefit of training personalized models for these unlabeled clients. In the perspective of incentives and fairness of clients the method also is not really convincing. 
- In the evaluation, the model used and the dataset used seems rather outdated, and easy ones and not sure how convincing the results actually are. Moreover, as mentioned above it seems like the data heterogeneity across clients will matter quite a lot here and the fact that this is not really explored in either in the theory or experiment section is concerning.

comment.value:
Thank you for your review. In the following, we hope to answer your question.


> First, if the labeled clients data does not match well of the unlabeled clients' data, which is often the case in federated learning due to data heterogeneity and cannot really be controlled since they are clients' private data, the performance I believe will largely suffer. 

That is correct, but it is a limitation of the learning setting itself, not of FLowDUP. No PFL method for unlabeled clients can learn good models if no statistical information is available about what good models for the unlabeled clients’ could be. Since unlabeled clients don’t have such information by definition, it has to be come from other, labeled, clients. The most natural assumption is that if two clients have similar marginal distributions, $D_i(X)$, then their conditionals, $D_i(Y|X)$, will also be similar, regardless if these clients actually do have labeled data or not. This is one example where labeled-to-unlabeled PFL (including FlowDUP) can be expected to work, and it often reflects the real-world. For example, two users who watched similar movies in the past probably have a similar taste in movies, even though, in principle, movie ratings are subjective, so personalization is crucial. 




> Moreover, it is rather unfair for the labeled clients to provide their training resource/data for the benefit of training personalized models for these unlabeled clients. In the perspective of incentives and fairness of clients the method also is not really convincing.

First, to clarify: in FlowDUP, the labelled clients do not directly train a personalized model for other clients. They are jointly training a hypernetwork that is used to generate their own models, as well as models for future unlabeled clients. In some sense, FlowDUP is more fair than previous labeled-to-unlabeled PFL methods, because at training time unlabeled clients can also help the learning process through their contributions to the regularization term. 

In general, however, we see your concern as orthogonal to our contribution. The starting point of our analysis is the setup where a number of clients are volunteering to learn jointly. Clients who are not willing to do so would have opted out previously and would simply not show up in our setup. The related question, how to incentivize or reward users to participate in federated learning has been discussed in a number of studies (e.g. [1],[2]), but we see these as outside of the scope of our work. 

[1] Y. Zhan et al.  "A Survey of Incentive Mechanism Design for Federated Learning," in IEEE Transactions on Emerging Topics in Computing, 2022

[2] A. Murhekar et al. “Incentives in Federated Learning: Equilibria, Dynamics, and Mechanisms for Welfare Maximization”, NeurIPS 2023.

> In the evaluation, the model used and the dataset used seems rather outdated, and easy ones and not sure how convincing the results actually are. Moreover, as mentioned above it seems like the data heterogeneity across clients will matter quite a lot here and the fact that this is not really explored in either in the theory or experiment section is concerning.

The models and datasets we are using are standard baselines in the literature, which also model to some extent different kinds of heterogeneity. We agree, though, that it would be desirable if new standard benchmarks for personalized federated learning would emerge. If you are aware of such efforts, we would be very happy to hear about them. 
Note that we actually expect FlowDUP to benefit from more complexity or more heterogeneity: the more expressive the learned networks are, the more prior methods struggle to avoid overfitting. FlowDUP’s additional use of non-labelled clients for regularization could allow the heterogeneity to be reflected better at training time.

We hope that our replies have addressed your concerns. If not, we will be happy to engage in a further discussion.

display_title: Official Review of Submission12191 by Reviewer Z1uj

summary.value: This paper addresses a critical limitation of existing personalized federated learning (PFL) methods—their reliance on labeled client data to generate personalized models—by proposing FLowDUP (Federated Low Dimensional Unlabeled Personalization), a framework enabling personalized model generation for unlabeled clients via a single forward pass on unlabeled data. FLowDUP trains a hypernetwork h that takes unlabeled client data as input and outputs low-dimensional subspace parameters \(v_i\). Full model parameters \(\theta_i\) are derived via \(\theta_i = \theta_0 + Pv_i\) (where P is a fixed random expansion matrix and \(\theta_0\) is an initial parameter), avoiding high-dimensional parameter transmission. The objective combines a loss L (evaluated on labeled clients to measure model quality) and a learnable regularizer \(\Omega\) (computed on all clients, including unlabeled ones, to prevent overfitting).

strengths.value:
1-FLowDUP directly addresses a well-identified pain point of PFL (unlabeled client incompatibility) with a non-trivial solution. Unlike prior hypernetwork-based methods (e.g., Amosy et al. 2024; Scott et al. 2024), it uses low-dimensional subspaces to enable on-device hypernetwork deployment and leverages unlabeled clients for training—two key innovations that distinguish it from related work.

2-It explicitly connects the regularizer \(\Omega\) and loss L to generalization performance, providing a mathematical justification for FLowDUP’s objective. This contrasts with many PFL works that lack theoretical guarantees for unlabeled clients.

3-Low-dimensional parameters reduce communication costs, the hypernetwork is lightweight for edge devices, and no client data is transmitted. This aligns with the core goals of federated learning (privacy, efficiency).

weaknesses.value:
1-FLowDUP fails when conditional distributions \(D_{i|Y|X}\) (label given input) differ across clients but marginal distributions \(D_{i|X}\) (input alone) are insufficient to infer predictive models—e.g., subjective tasks like product recommendations or sentiment analysis. The authors acknowledge this but provide no mitigation strategies, restricting the method’s real-world applicability.

2-The default \(k=10^4\) is chosen empirically, with no theoretical analysis of how k relates to dataset heterogeneity, model architecture, or performance. While experiments show k correlates with accuracy, the lack of a principled way to select k (e.g., via the generalization bound) reduces FLowDUP’s usability.

3-All experiments use the \(pfl-research\) simulation library—there is no validation on actual edge devices (e.g., smartphones, IoT sensors). The authors claim low computational cost, but simulated efficiency may not translate to real hardware (e.g., memory constraints, latency).

The authors acknowledge this but provide no mitigation strategies, restricting the method’s real-world applicability.

comment.value:
Thank you for your review. In the following, we hope to answer your question.

> FLowDUP fails when conditional distributions (D_{i|Y|X}) (label given input) differ across clients but marginal distributions (D_{i|X}) (input alone) are insufficient to infer predictive models—e.g., subjective tasks like product recommendations or sentiment analysis. The authors acknowledge this but provide no mitigation strategies, restricting the method’s real-world applicability.

This is correct, and we explicitly mention it in the paper (lines 480-485). However, as we discuss there, no learning method can produce personalized models for unlabeled clients if the clients’ marginals $D_i(X)$ contains no information about their conditionals $D_i(Y|X)$. This is a limitation of the learning setting itself, not of FLowDUP.

> The default (k=10^4) is chosen empirically, with no theoretical analysis of how k relates to dataset heterogeneity, model architecture, or performance. While experiments show k correlates with accuracy, the lack of a principled way to select k (e.g., via the generalization bound) reduces FLowDUP’s usability.

As shown in Table 4, the bigger $k$, the better the results we get, as the model would have more capacity to learn, and the regularization prevents overfitting. The only trade-off is communication cost vs $k$, and our suggested recipe for choosing this value is to choose it as big as your communication budget allows it. A core contribution of our paper, we show that small values of $k$ still yield good performance, so FlowDUP works even in the communication-limited regime (as desirable for FL). 

> All experiments use the (pfl-research) simulation library—there is no validation on actual edge devices (e.g., smartphones, IoT sensors). The authors claim low computational cost, but simulated efficiency may not translate to real hardware (e.g., memory constraints, latency).

We follow the common practice here. For academic research, it is generally not feasible to deploy models on actual user devices. It would also make the evaluation not reproducible. Note that the library we use is published by Apple, and papers from such a big company also use simulations. We believe it is not reasonable to expect these experiments from our paper.

About the computational cost, we mean this in comparison to prior hypernetwork-based PFL methods that output the complete model parameter vector. If we denote the number of model parameter by $d$ and the number of hidden units before the last layer by $p$, the final layer would have $p \times d$ parameters, whereas for FlowDUP it would be $p \times k$.
For example, suppose d=12M (e.g., ResNet-18), p=256, k=10^4. Prior work would need 256×12M ≈ 3.07 billion weights (∼12.3 GB in fp32) just in the hypernetwork’s output layer. In contrast, FlowDUP only requires 256×10^4 ≈ 2.56 million weights (∼10 MB). This is what we mean by “orders of magnitude smaller”, and by the reduction of communication and computational costs.

We hope that our replies have addressed your concerns. If not, we will be happy to engage in a further discussion.

display_title: Official Review of Submission12191 by Reviewer dN3E

summary.value: The paper proposes a PFL method called FLowDUP that generates a client-specific model using only unlabeled data. FLowDUP employs a hypernetwork to produce low-dimensional subspace parameters, which are expanded via a fixed random matrix to yield the full model. Its training objective combines a labeled-client loss and an unlabeled-client regularizer, theoretically supported by a new transductive multi-task PAC-Bayesian generalization bound. Experiments across serveral widely-used datasets show improved performance compared with baselines such as FedAvg, FedProx, and ATP.

strengths.value:
1. Addressing personalization for unlabeled clients is a relatively unexplored area in PFL.
2. The paper introduces a new transductive multi-task PAC-Bayesian bound that motivates the objective and gives its proof.
3. The low-dimensional subspace formulation has the potential to reduce communication and computation costs in federated settings.

weaknesses.value:
1. The proposed method is built upon the foundations of regulation-based and hypernetwork-based personalized federated learning (PFL). However, the related work section does not provide an adequate review or a clear comparison between prior methods and the proposed approach.
2. The paper uses the hypernet for personalization which is not a new idea. Besides, the authors emphasize that the proposed method can handle federated learning with labeled data, yet there is no direct comparison with existing hypernetwork-based PFL approaches, such as [1] and [2].
3. If FedAvg cannot be trained without labels, how was it used for comparison? If FedAvg was trained with labeled data but the proposed method used unlabeled data, how is this comparison fair and meaningful?
4. The paper claims that the proposed approach is computationally and communication efficient, yet no experiments or quantitative evidence are presented to substantiate this claim.
5. The writing and structural focus of the paper could be improved. While substantial space (including Appendix A) is devoted to PAC-Bayes theory, its direct connection to the proposed method is not clearly articulated and should be elaborated. Conversely, the discussion of basic federated learning concepts is overly detailed and could be condensed.

[1] Shamsian, A. et al. “Personalized Federated Learning Using Hypernetworks.” ICML, 2021.

[2] Yang, Z. et al. “Hypernetwork-Based Physics-Driven Personalized Federated Learning for CT Imaging.” IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems, 2023.

questions.value:
1. What is the detailed form of the regularization term $\psi_r$ in implementation, will the authors make their code public?
2. The paper claims that FLowDUP supports training with unlabeled data, but all experimental datasets are public labeled datasets. How were the results in Tables 1 and 2 obtained, were the training data labeled, unlabeled, or partially labeled?
3. What was the data splitting scheme between labeled and unlabeled clients?

comment.value:
Thank you for your review. In the following, we hope to answer your questions.


> The proposed method is built upon the foundations of regulation-based and hypernetwork-based personalized federated learning (PFL). However, the related work section does not provide an adequate review or a clear comparison between prior methods and the proposed approach.

Could you please clarify your concerns? Our setup is PFL for clients without labeled training data. We compare with related methods in lines 435-455, out of which lines 440-450 cover hypernetwork-based approaches. This includes a discussion of how FlowDup differs from those: it can benefit from unlabeled clients at training time, and it saves communication cost via its low-dimensional representation. Do you have other specific methods in mind we should have discussed? 

We do not discuss PFL methods that only work for labeled clients (such as [1] and [2]). Clearly, there are many of those but they are not applicable in our setting. If such a discussion is what you were suggesting, we’ll be happy to add it. 


> The paper uses the hypernet for personalization which is not a new idea. 

We do not claim novelty of hypernetworks for PFL, indeed we cite prior work for it. The novelty of our work (on the hypernetwork side) is the low-dimensional parametrization which allows transferring and running hypernetworks on the clients. This was not possible before because standard hypernetworks tends to be orders of magnitude bigger than the networks they produced. 

> Besides, the authors emphasize that the proposed method can handle federated learning with labeled data, yet there is no direct comparison with existing hypernetwork-based PFL approaches, such as [1] and [2].

Like every PFL method for unlabeled clients, FlowDUP can also create models for labeled clients (by simply ignoring the labels). This is not a focus of our work, though, and we do not expect FlowDUP (or any other unlabeled method) to work better than methods that do exploit client labels for model generation. We are not aware that we would emphasize FlowDUP’s ability to create models for labeled clients, but if you let us know which statement you refer to, we will be happy to adjust it. 

What we do emphasize is that some labeled clients are needed at training time, because otherwise there is no signal for any supervised learning.

> If FedAvg cannot be trained without labels, how was it used for comparison? If FedAvg was trained with labeled data but the proposed method used unlabeled data, how is this comparison fair and meaningful?

Let us clarify our setting (see e.g. lines 112-114): at training time, some clients have labels (and some might not). FedAvg can be trained using the labeled clients. The result is a single (not personalized) model that can be applied to any future input data, including that on unlabeled future clients. 

FlowDUP is trained also using the labeled clients, but additionally it can exploit unlabeled clients at training time, which FedAvg cannot. FlowDUP creates a hypernetwork that takes a client’s unlabeled data as input and outputs a personalized model for that client. 

> The paper claims that the proposed approach is computationally and communication efficient, yet no experiments or quantitative evidence are presented to substantiate this claim.

This statement is in comparison to other hypernetwork-based methods, such as [1] and [2], which, if they sent the whole hypernetwork, they would have a massive communication cost, and if they don’t sent, they would have to do a multiple step communication per round with an advanced optimization which also sends the encoding of the client data which violates privacy.

> The writing and structural focus of the paper could be improved. While substantial space (including Appendix A) is devoted to PAC-Bayes theory, its direct connection to the proposed method is not clearly articulated and should be elaborated. Conversely, the discussion of basic federated learning concepts is overly detailed and could be condensed.

Thank you for the suggestions. Our discussion in lines 253-269 was meant to describe how our objective functions, the learned regularizer, and the role of unlabelled clients directly come from our generalization bounds and motivate different parts of our algorithms theoretically. We’ll be happy to clarify this further.

comment.value:
> What is the detailed form of the regularization term $\psi_r$  in implementation, will the authors make their code public?

Yes, we will, of course, make our code public for the camera-ready version.

The regularization term contributes to the loss exactly as a L2 regularizer. In pytorch:

    loss = 0.5 * output_regularization * nn.MSELoss(reduction='mean')(
        target_params,
        regularization_parameters
    )

where output_regularization is $\lambda$, target_param is $v_i$ and regularization_parameters is the $k$-dim parameter vector $\psi_r$ (see Eq. 6)

> The paper claims that FLowDUP supports training with unlabeled data, but all experimental datasets are public labeled datasets. How were the results in Tables 1 and 2 obtained, were the training data labeled, unlabeled, or partially labeled?

We follow standard practice here. For the purpose of reporting benchmark results, it is necessary to use datasets with ground truth information. All tested algorithms, however, only have access to the setting described above: at training time, a fraction of clients have labelled data ($p$ in the tables) the others are unlabeled. The algorithms are free to make use of the clients any way they can. For the reported numbers, we evaluate how well the learned systems work on previously unseen unlabeled clients. For each such client, we generate a model (the global one for FedAvg, the personalized one for other methods) and evaluate its quality of the validation ground truth data (which the methods do not have access to). 

> What was the data splitting scheme between labeled and unlabeled clients?

We choose a fraction of clients ($p$) at random to have labelled data, and we drop the labelled data of the remaining clients. 


We hope that our replies have addressed your concerns. If not, we will be happy to engage in a further discussion.

Thank you for your detailed responses. Most of my concerns have been addressed, but I would like to suggest a few areas for further clarification.

1. While I understand the emphasis on the low-dimensional hypernetwork approach and its efficiency, I believe a stronger comparison with existing hypernetwork-based methods, such as [1] and [2], particularly in scenarios with both labeled and unlabeled data, would be beneficial.

2. I appreciate the clarification on computational and communication efficiency. To further support this claim, I suggest including empirical evidence comparing the communication and computation costs of your method with other baselines.

3. Regarding the statement, “we do not expect FlowDUP (or any other unlabeled method) to work better than methods that do exploit client labels for model generation,” I find it counterproductive in scenarios where labeled data is abundant. If labeled data must be discarded to use this method, it undermines the value of federated learning, especially when labeled data could improve performance with other methods. In such cases, fully leveraging labeled data would be more practical than using a method that disregards it.

Considering these points and the feedback from other reviewers, I believe my rating accurately reflects the paper's quality, and I will maintain my current rating.

display_title: Meta Review of Submission12191 by Area Chair 79jq

summary.value:
This paper proposes FLowDUP, a personalized federated learning approach that generates low-dimensional personalized models for clients with only unlabeled data, motivated by a new transductive multi-task PAC-Bayesian generalization bound. The problem setting, personalization for unlabeled clients, is timely and important, and the proposed method is technically interesting and promising.

However, despite these strengths, there are **significant unresolved concerns** regarding (i) the **clarity and novelty of the theoretical contribution**, and (ii) the **adequacy of the experimental evaluation for a personalized federated learning setting**. In particular, the empirical comparisons and baselines do not yet convincingly support the paper’s claims in the targeted regime.

**Recommendation:** Reject

While FLowDUP is a promising and potentially impactful idea, the current version does not yet provide a sufficiently clear theoretical contribution nor a comprehensive and appropriate experimental evaluation for personalized federated learning. Addressing the above issues, particularly by clarifying the novelty of the theory and conducting a stronger, more standard personalized-FL-focused empirical study, would significantly strengthen the work and could make it suitable for acceptance in a future iteration.

reviewer_concerns.value:
Below, I have included concerns raised by the reviewer, as well as concerns identified during my own review of the paper.

**Concerns that were partially addressed:**

* The authors provided additional clarification on the training setup with labeled vs. unlabeled clients and expanded comparisons in the appendix, including some hypernetwork-based methods and additional ablations.
* Reviewer questions regarding implementation details (e.g., the regularization term, labeled/unlabeled client splits) were answered clearly.
* One reviewer (dN3E) ultimately felt their concerns were sufficiently addressed and recommended acceptance after the rebuttal.

**Major concerns that remain outstanding:**

1. **Unclear theoretical novelty and positioning.**
   While the paper introduces a transductive multi-task PAC-Bayesian bound and claims it motivates the learning objective, it remains unclear to me what is fundamentally new compared to existing PAC-Bayes analyses for multi-task or transductive learning, and how essential this theory is beyond post-hoc justification. The connection between the bound and the algorithm is not articulated with enough precision, and this concern is only partially addressed in the rebuttal. As a result, the theoretical contribution remains ambiguous in terms of novelty and necessity.

2. **Mismatch between the experimental regime and the baselines used.**
   The proposed method is inherently personalized, producing a distinct model for each client. However, much of the comparison is against baselines such as FedAvg and FedProx, which are fundamentally non-personalized and still rely on a single global model. FedProx is designed for non-IID splits (e.g., each client receives data from only two classes), whereas a single model should be suitable for all clients. This makes it difficult to assess whether other personalized design choices could be effective. I realize that these models require access to labeled data, but it would be beneficial to see at least an evaluation on the subset of clients that do have labeled data. 

3. **Missing standard personalized federated learning baselines.**
   A key weakness of the experimental evaluation is the absence (or only very limited inclusion, mostly in appendices) of widely accepted personalized FL baselines, such as:

   * FedAvg / FedProx with client-side fine-tuning,
   * APFL (Smith et al., 2017),
   * Per-FedAvg (Fallah et al., 2020),
   * Ditto (Li et al., 2021),
   * DPFL (Kharrat et al., 2025).

   Some of these were added late or partially in response to reviewer comments, but not integrated into the main experimental narrative. Given that the method explicitly targets personalization, comparisons against these baselines are essential and should be central rather than peripheral.

4. **Limited realism and scale of experiments.**
   Although several benchmark datasets are included, the evaluation still relies heavily on relatively small-scale image classification tasks and synthetic heterogeneity patterns. More extensive experiments (i.e., using larger models, more realistic client heterogeneity, and real-world FL scenarios) would be necessary to convincingly demonstrate robustness and practical relevance.

reviewer_scores.value: Based on my reading, the reviewer dN3E would keep their weak accept score. For the other two reviewers, although they recommend a weak rejection that I expect to be kept, their reviews are of low quality. I mainly rely on feedback from reviewer dN3E and my own reading of the paper when making the recommendation.
